question: Under the Navigation Rules, what must the give-way vessel do if its early course change does not appear to be resolving a crossing situation?
choice_a: Take further, more substantial action, such as slowing, stopping, or reversing, well before risk of collision becomes immediate
choice_b: Hold its original course regardless of the developing risk
choice_c: Sound the danger signal and continue at the same speed
choice_d: Wait for the stand-on vessel to act first
explanation: If an early, obvious course change by the give-way vessel does not appear to be resolving the risk of collision, the Navigation Rules require it to take further and more substantial action -- such as slowing, stopping, or reversing -- well before the situation becomes critical.

question: Under the Navigation Rules, at what point does even a stand-on vessel have a duty to take action to avoid a collision?
choice_a: When it becomes apparent the give-way vessel is not taking appropriate action, and collision cannot be avoided by the give-way vessel's actions alone
choice_b: A stand-on vessel never has any duty to act, no matter what happens
choice_c: Only after a collision has already occurred
choice_d: Only if the stand-on vessel is a sailboat
explanation: While a stand-on vessel should generally maintain course and speed, the Navigation Rules require it to take whatever action will best avoid collision once it becomes apparent the give-way vessel is not taking appropriate action on its own.

question: In the standard right-of-way hierarchy taught in boating safety courses, how does a vessel engaged in commercial fishing with gear deployed generally rank relative to an ordinary recreational powerboat?
choice_a: The commercial fishing vessel generally ranks higher, since its deployed gear restricts its ability to maneuver freely
choice_b: Commercial fishing vessels always rank lowest in the hierarchy
choice_c: Recreational powerboats always outrank commercial fishing vessels
choice_d: There is no distinction between the two vessel types under the Navigation Rules
explanation: A vessel engaged in commercial fishing with nets, lines, or trawls actually deployed generally ranks above an ordinary recreational powerboat in the right-of-way hierarchy, because its gear substantially restricts its ability to maneuver to avoid other traffic.

question: What is the standard definition of a vessel "not under command," a category that ranks near the top of the right-of-way hierarchy?
choice_a: A vessel that, through some exceptional circumstance such as mechanical failure, is unable to maneuver as required by the Navigation Rules and therefore cannot keep out of the way of another vessel
choice_b: Any vessel whose operator has not completed a boater education course
choice_c: A vessel that is simply anchored for the night
choice_d: A vessel operating without a current registration decal
explanation: A vessel "not under command" is one that, through some exceptional circumstance like engine failure or loss of steering, cannot maneuver as required and therefore cannot keep out of the way of other vessels -- placing it near the top of the right-of-way hierarchy since it has the least ability to avoid a collision.

question: Once a vessel has begun overtaking another vessel and become the overtaking vessel, does its duty to keep clear ever transfer back to the vessel being overtaken during that pass?
choice_a: No -- the overtaking vessel remains the give-way vessel for the entire passing maneuver, until it is finally past and clear
choice_b: Yes, the duty automatically shifts once the overtaking vessel draws even with the other vessel
choice_c: The duty shifts back and forth every 30 seconds during the maneuver
choice_d: Neither vessel has any duty once an overtaking situation begins
explanation: Under the Navigation Rules, once a vessel becomes the overtaking vessel, it remains the give-way vessel for the entire passing maneuver, and that obligation does not shift back to the vessel being overtaken until the overtaking vessel is finally past and clear.
